statements.venue: NewsNation interview ("The Hill Sunday"), reported by The Hill
statements.quote: If this is about building something that's a weapon of mass destruction, let's get on top of it.
statements.context: Asked about warnings from AI company leaders and a former Anthropic researcher; he was discussing hostile countries such as Iran getting hold of advanced AI and called for federal safeguards to keep AI out of the wrong hands.
statements.reason: Conditionally accepts that AI could amount to a weapon of mass destruction and says Congress should act, but the danger he names is misuse by hostile states, so it is C under the misuse-only ruling.

statements.venue: NewsNation interview ("The Hill Sunday"), reported by The Hill
statements.quote: when somebody says it's going to lead to world destruction, well, what is that?
statements.context: Responding to warnings that AI could cause catastrophe; he said Congress should get the facts and specifics before legislating.
statements.reason: Relays others' warning of world destruction without endorsing it; he asks for specifics rather than dismissing it, so C, though it sits near D.

statements.quote: I’m taking the CEOs of artificial intelligence tech companies seriously. I’m not in a position to validate whether or not their concerns are real.
statements.context: Responding to AI company leaders' warnings about AI safety, in a story that also quotes a University of Nebraska Omaha professor on extinction-level risk.
statements.reason: Says he takes AI executives' safety warnings seriously but does not adopt them as his own view, which is C.

statements.quote: I want to go on a fact-finding mission. You know, some in Congress, they want to pass a bill. It’s kind of like, shoot, ready, aim. Like, what exactly a problem are we trying to solve here?
statements.context: Explaining that Congress should study AI risk before legislating.
statements.reason: Skeptical of rushing to legislate but does not dismiss catastrophic risk itself, so D rather than F.

statements.quote: Congress has a responsibility to ensure consumers have commonsense protections from artificial intelligence without putting the brakes on American innovation.
statements.context: Statement celebrating House passage of the Ratepayer Protection Act, which he co-sponsored, to keep data center energy costs from being passed on to consumers.
statements.reason: Speaks of consumer protections from AI and data center electricity costs, with no catastrophic risk acknowledged.

statements.venue: Op-ed in Townhall (reposted as a column on his official site)
statements.quote: We as Americans must take a hard look at how technology, AI, and social media are polarizing our country and influencing us individually.
statements.context: Column on free speech and the rule of law after the killing of Charlie Kirk.
statements.reason: Concerns AI's role in political polarization, not catastrophic risk.

slowdown.note: No statement for or against slowing frontier AI development for safety reasons; his 'shoot, ready, aim' remark criticises rushing a bill, and 'without putting the brakes on American innovation' is about consumer protections and data centers, so neither is counted as 'no'.

pause.note: No statement found on pausing frontier AI development.

intl.note: No statement found on coordinating with China on the pace of AI development.

rsi.note: No statement found on banning self-improving AI.

record: Co-sponsored the Ratepayer Protection Act (H.R. 9340), which passed the House, to keep data center energy costs from being passed on to consumers.
grade_reason: In September 2026 he said that if AI amounts to a weapon of mass destruction Congress should 'get on top of it' (misuse by hostile states only, so C) and that he takes AI executives' warnings seriously without validating them (relayed, so C). He is skeptical of rushing legislation but does not dismiss catastrophic risk, so no F reduction.
notes: All six required web searches ran this time, plus one on the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (7 in total); the earlier attempt's searches were all refused. The Hill article (2026-09-13, by Max Rego) was read through a page-fetch tool that returns extracted text rather than the raw page, and it shortens long quotes, so the two Hill quotes are short exact passages as returned by that tool; a reviewer should confirm them against the page. A direct download of The Hill page was blocked. The WOWT quotes were checked against the downloaded page text. Paraphrases left out: The Hill says he wants federal safeguards to keep AI from 'falling into the wrong hands', that AI company leaders should be 'answering questions' on safety and risks, that he wants the U.S. to build 'massive wealth' through AI, and he said 'I mean, this is bigger than shutting down a cellular network' (about adversary misuse; not included as a separate statement). The 'world destruction' quote and the 'shoot, ready, aim' quote could be read as mildly skeptical of catastrophic risk; I judged neither to be dismissal (F) because he asks for specifics and says he is taking the warnings seriously. No source shows him sponsoring or co-sponsoring the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (H.R. 10538, introduced 24 September 2026; listed cosponsors seen were Democrats), or leading any House letter on AI risk. From the earlier attempt: his official site was read directly (160 press releases from 13 February 2025 to 9 October 2026 and columns from June 2024 to September 2026); the only other AI item, a 2025-09-02 press release announcing an 'AI and Banking' panel at his Flyover Fintech conference, was dropped to keep D statements to three. Hearing remarks and floor speeches were not specifically checked.
